opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, MIT was less a calculated decision and more something I'd been quietly drawn to for years. Growing up in China, I was deep into math competitions, and MIT kept coming up as this almost mythical place where people who loved problems for their own sake ended up. I'd read about the problem-solving culture there, the idea that you could walk down the Infinite Corridor and bump into someone working on something wild at two in the morning. That really resonated with me.

What attracted me most, I think, was the sense of freedom. In a lot of systems you're on a fixed track: you take the exam, you get sorted, you follow the path. MIT seemed to say, "Here are incredibly hard problems and incredibly smart people. Go figure out what you care about." For a teenager who loved math but also wanted to explore physics, computing, and how ideas connect, that was very appealing.

So studying abroad wasn't really about leaving something behind. It was about going toward a particular kind of intellectual environment. Of course, it was also scary. I was young, far from family, and adjusting to a new language and culture. But I remember feeling that if I didn't try, I'd always wonder what kind of mathematician, or person, I could have become in that setting.

Looking back, that choice shaped almost everything after it. The way I think about research, about collaboration, and even about starting something new all goes back to that MIT spirit: take on the hard problem, and don't wait for permission.

r001.rationale: She says studying abroad was about going toward a particular intellectual environment and identifies MIT as the place she had been drawn to for years, indicating a specific desire to attend MIT.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started with something much more romantic than a career calculation. When I was in middle school in Guangzhou, I came across the story of Richard Feynman and the whole culture of physicists and mathematicians who treated hard problems like play. MIT was the place that kept showing up in those stories. So in my mind it wasn't really a school, it was almost a mythology, a place where people stayed up all night arguing about ideas because they couldn't help themselves.

At the time I was doing math competitions, and I was good at them, but I had this growing sense that competition math was a bit of a closed world. You solve the problem, you get the medal, and then the problem is gone. What I wanted was to be somewhere the problems were open, where nobody knew the answer yet. And the people I read about who lived that way, a lot of them had passed through MIT.

So the decision to go abroad wasn't really "I want to leave China." It was "I want to be in that specific room." I think that distinction mattered a lot for how I prepared. I wasn't optimizing for a brand name across the board. I was pretty single-minded about one place, which my parents found slightly alarming, because it's obviously not a safe strategy.

And I'll admit, when I actually got there, the reality was both less and more than the myth. Less, because it's a real institution with real bureaucracy and a lot of very tired undergraduates. More, because the thing I'd imagined, that sense of people genuinely obsessed, turned out to be true. My first problem set in 18.100 made me feel like I'd never really done math before. That was humbling and also exactly what I'd been looking for.

r001.rationale: She says the decision to go abroad was really about wanting to be in “that specific room” at MIT, and that she was single-minded about one place.

astra-6.text: MIT gave me a concrete reason to consider studying abroad. I was drawn to the possibility of being around people who were deeply curious about math and science, in an environment where I could explore those interests more fully. So my thinking became less about going abroad in itself and more about finding the kind of intellectual community I wanted to be part of.

r001.rationale: The response says MIT prompted her to consider studying abroad, but frames her underlying motivation as finding a curious intellectual community rather than communicating a desire to attend MIT specifically.

sol-6.1.text: MIT was a big part of what drew me to studying abroad. I was excited by the idea of being somewhere where people really love math and science, where you can explore difficult questions with others who share that curiosity. So, for me, studying abroad was less about going to another country and more about finding that kind of intellectual environment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says MIT was a big part of what drew her to studying abroad and describes seeking that intellectual environment, linking the apparent desire to study abroad specifically to MIT.
